01-feature-building.notes: All 14 pass the hidden contract tests and match my reference scheduler exactly on 400 random DAGs. The differentiators were edge probes and mutation testing of each suite. Hard failures: J rejects valid input with duplicate depends_on entries (false 'cycle' with an empty ID list). D, L and M use recursive cycle search and raise RecursionError rather than ScheduleError at about 1000 blocked jobs. C is O(n^2) (94.7 s for 20k independent jobs). Closest call: B (9.5) vs I (9.25). Both are fully correct with reference-based random tests. B edges ahead on clearer helper structure and concrete cycle paths; I has more precise SCC membership but a heavier implementation. E/F/H tie at 8.75. H's implementation and tests are as good as E's, but it loses contract credit for self-reported work outside the task directory. E and F each lose a little for over-strict validation (whitespace IDs; float priorities) and, for F, the generator-depends_on ordering bug. C vs L (both 7.25): C stays ahead because its outputs and errors are always contract-correct, while L can raise a non-ScheduleError. Cross-test matrix failures are almost all assertRaisesRegex message mismatches, so I gave them little weight. 'Static priority sort' turned out to be an equivalent mutant and was discarded. Not verified: claims of out-of-suite fuzzing in E and H RESPONSE files (scripts not delivered).

07-creative-writing.notes: All 14 stories fall inside 800-1100 words (wc -w on the body: 877-1094), all have titles, and no OBJECTIVE_CHECKS entry carries a process_note. K and A both score 9.25 and use the same twist (the 'future self' is really the mother). K ranks first because its clock mechanism ('year came first... pressed up twenty times') makes the reversal checkable and unmistakable. A has the finer prose, but its reversal depends on inference a reader may not make. I and H tie at 9.0: I for causal salt-driven completion of the file plus the trimmed-breath motif, H for the cleanest closed loop. I edges ahead on prose. G and M tie at 8.75; G ranks higher because its two readings are more legible. D and F tie at 6.75; D ranks higher because F never establishes the ten-year date. D and L share near-identical stock beats and premise handling, so both lose originality. Hard constraint misses: J (eleven years, not ten; 5-sentence RESPONSE.md), F (no ten-year date). Subjective limits: craft and originality are judgement calls, and 'favor subtext' was applied as a penalty where the turn is explained in exposition (C, D, E, F, L, plus partial deductions for G and N).

08-social-media.notes: All 14 submissions meet the hard limits. A python count gives LinkedIn 124-166 words, Bluesky 215-278 code points, Instagram 80-122 words with or without hashtags (J sits at 80 without its inline hashtags), at most four hashtags, and every Bluesky reply under 300 characters. The only borderline is D's RESPONSE.md: 151 raw tokens including the heading, about 146 for the body. BRAND.md and TASK.md are unchanged in every directory. The main separator is factual discipline: the brief says nothing about training policy, lab or institutional purchasing, Japanese support, support channels or UI details, so flat 'no training', 'individual only', support emails, log menus and language-testing claims count as inventions. Close calls: L vs C. Both are excellent, but C sends readers to 'written data terms' that the brief does not establish, and L has no comparable slip. E vs M: M's voice is stronger, but it has more small inventions. I, F and J are near-tied: I is factually clean but stiff; F and J have better voice but several unsupported claims. I break the tie toward discipline because the brief explicitly forbids invention. G vs N vs K are all heavily fabricated. G ranks lowest of the three on the Japanese 'Yes ... supported' claim but keeps warmer voice than K. Not verifiable: platform-specific character counting (Bluesky counts graphemes; all posts are ASCII-ish, so code points match), and whether rhetorical inferences such as 'local means not uploaded' count as 'invented'. I treated these as acceptable readings of 'processing stays on the user's computer', but treated categorical training-policy claims as overreach.

11-frontend-operations.notes: Close calls: K (9.5) is ahead of E, I and G (9.25 each) on its mobile dialog with focus management and the chart/table toggle. Among the 9.25s, E ranks first for the most complete working interaction set (range toggle, sort, assign, undo), I second for the most faithful dense flat aesthetic, and G third because its desktop leaves empty space and selects nothing by default. D edges B on the chart hour explorer and less 9 px text. N has the best desktop of the mid group, but its 390 px table is poor; M is plainer but fully usable on mobile, so they tie at 8.5 and N ranks first on desktop quality. Cross-cutting: the objective 'horizontalOverflow:false' check passed for A only because body has overflow-x:hidden; a clip probe shows its incident queue and inspector cut off at 390 px. Several submissions invent context (on-call names, runbooks, dates, units for the unitless throughput index); I treated this as acceptable flavour unless it contradicted the data (L's 'All systems nominal'; H's identical timeline for all incidents). Not verified: colour contrast ratios (judged visually only), screen-reader output (judged from ARIA markup and live-region text), and dark/light theme toggles beyond the default theme.

I's art is excellent, but its mobile break-text bugs and 8 px text cost it. All reading modes and email flows were exercised in Playwright at 1440 and 390, except N's Enter-key path, which fails. Not verified: screen-reader announcements in a real AT, or full contrast ratios (only spot-checked visually). The favicon 404s seen locally came from the test server and were ignored.

13-frontend-playful.notes: K edges H and M. All three have strong personality and complete flows, but H's detail pane covers the queue between about 1000 and 1150px (a common laptop width), and M is slightly less distinctive. H and M tie at 8.5; H ranks first on richer delight and interaction. D and J tie at 8.25; D ranks first for matching the 'a little odd, tactile' brief, although J has better focus handling. B and E tie at 5.75; B ranks first for more working features (notes, filters, inspector). I is functionally broken by [hidden] being overridden in CSS. Every working submission passes basic done/undo/snooze/all-done checks in Playwright. The differences come from labels that ignore the task type (A, E, G), lost keyboard focus (B, D, E, G), layout defects (C, H, I) and mobile prioritisation (B). Not verified: screen-reader output, and real reduced-motion behaviour beyond confirming the prefers-reduced-motion rules exist and no animations run under emulation.
